metadata.title: Early career teacher retention intention: Individual, school and country characteristics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2), with schools selected using systematic two-stage random sampling with probability proportional to size within explicit strata by country. TALIS applies complex survey design features (stratification and clustering at school level), but the manuscript does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) in the multilevel regression estimation. The authors estimate multilevel linear regression models in Stata SE 16.0 and focus on variance decomposition and ICCs across teacher, school, and country levels, which partially addresses clustering through the multilevel structure rather than through survey-weighted estimation. Because the paper does not document weight application, results should be interpreted as model-based associations under the assumed sampling design, with potential sensitivity to weighting choices.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is teachers’ expected career duration (a survey response), not a cognitive achievement score generated via PVs. The paper also does not describe any PV-based scaling for the outcome, consistent with TALIS being a teacher survey rather than an achievement test. Missing data handling is addressed via case deletion: the authors state they deleted cases with missing values for variables included in the analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data come from TALIS 2018 (48 countries/economies), restricted to lower secondary education (ISCED 2) and further restricted to a European-focused set plus selected high-achieving Asian and North-American systems. Early-career teachers (ECTs) are defined as teachers with no more than 5 years of teaching experience. Teachers older than 45 years are excluded. The multilevel analyses include 31 countries/regions, with Belgium’s two regional educational systems analyzed separately (Flemish community and French-speaking community). The analytic sample is obtained after deleting cases with missing values for one or more variables included in the analyses (listwise deletion). For country-level model 9, the country sample is reduced from 31 to 25 because some country-level characteristics from part A are not available for all countries.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged Gender, Age (grand-mean centered), Teaching first choice to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This peer-reviewed study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2) to model expected career duration as a proxy for early-career teacher (ECT) retention intention. The analytic sample comprises 11,613 ECTs nested in 3,998 lower secondary schools across 31 countries/regions (Belgium’s two communities analyzed separately), with listwise deletion of cases missing any analysis variables and an additional reduction to 25 countries for model 9 due to missing country-level part-A indicators. The authors estimate nine-stage multilevel linear regression models (teacher, school, and country levels) rather than machine-learning prediction; therefore, no ML accuracy/AUC metrics are reported. Key results show that selection mechanisms (“becoming a teacher”) explain the largest share of variance, with model 9 explaining 17.2% overall variance (teacher 14.0%, school 13.1%, country 48.9% relative to the restricted unconditional model). Notably, higher starting salaries (b=0.25, p<0.001) and mandatory competitive exams (b=0.15, p<0.05) at the country level, and intrinsic motivation and teaching as first choice at the teacher level, are associated with longer expected teaching careers. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal claims) and reliance on subjective intention measures. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for the ML-specific schema because the paper does not train or evaluate any machine-learning predictive models; it uses multilevel linear regression to estimate associations. Consequently, main_findings is left empty (no ML target-variable prediction results with ML performance metrics), and ml_techniques contains no algorithms. The study is still empirical and provides multilevel regression coefficients and variance decomposition, but these do not map to the required ML StructuredFinding rows.
